next_steps: Schedule 2-week pilot run on Dedicated nodes (tentative week of 2026-04-27)
Share SOC2 + architecture diagram and VPC checklist
action_items: Lena: email cost-sim and SOC2 docs by 2026-04-12
Marcus: propose pilot cluster sizing and latency targets by 2026-04-16
Tomás: provide real qps distribution and 90/95/99 latencies by 2026-04-14
summary: Redwood AE/SE walked Avalon Diagnostics through an Optimize-style simulation focused on prefetch/prefix KV cache and concurrency batching to reduce per-token cost while maintaining 95th pct latency SLOs. Customer provided stack context (on-prem Kubernetes + private VPC) and primary constraints are PII data residency, 100 ms 95th latency target for critical flows, and budget target ~40% lower than current baseline. Agreed next steps: send cost model spreadsheet, run a two-week pilot on Dedicated with sample traces, and share security artifacts.
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-11
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Lena Ortiz (Redwood AE), Marcus Ng (Redwood SE), Ivy Chen (Redwood SA), Priya Shah (Avalon Head of Data), Tomás Rivera (Avalon Dir ML Infra), Ellen Park (Avalon CTO), Rashid Ahmed (Avalon SRE)

[00:00] Lena Ortiz: hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh, we can probably just kick off, super excited to walk through the prefetch + concurrency sim today. does this time still work?
[00:07] Priya Shah: yes, thanks Lena. should be good, we've got about 40 minutes.
[00:11] Marcus Ng: cool, i'll share my screen in a sec, but quick agenda: short context, run through cost-sim assumptions, show batch/prefetch scenarios, then recommended config and next steps. sound ok?
[00:21] Ellen Park: sounds good, want to make sure we touch on data residency and SLOs up front.
[00:25] Lena Ortiz: absolutely. thanks for flagging.

[00:30] Marcus Ng: quick context from Redwood side — we usually model three levers: batching (concurrency), prefix/KV cache hit rate, and model variant (full fp16 vs 4-bit quant). the sim ties those to per-token unit costs and p95 latency.
[00:41] Tomás Rivera: just to be clear, Avalon is running customer-sensitive ingestion on-prem currently, with a VPC peering plan for private deployment. we can't send raw PII out to hosted endpoints. so private deployment or dedicated nodes in our VPC is preferred.
[00:53] Ivy Chen: noted — we have Private (VPC) deployment and Dedicated reserved pools that can live in a customer VPC; we also have HSM/KMS integrations for keying. we'll include that in the security packet.

[01:07] Priya Shah: for this exercise, our main use case is document classification and entity extraction inside clinical notes. median prompt length 120 tokens, response 30 tokens. bursty QPS with peaks during batch ingest windows; baseline p95 today ~120 ms on your current infra with our previous self-hosted runtime. cost target: reduce token cost by ~40% across the pipeline.
[01:31] Marcus Ng: that's helpful... okay i'll pull up the sim. so baseline we set at no prefetch, concurrency 4 per GPU, fp16 model — baseline cost per 1k tokens = $X (placeholder), p95 120 ms. then we run scenarios: a) prefix KV only, b) prefetch (background warm) with sessionized keys, c) higher batching/concurrency with adaptive delay.

[02:05] [Screen share starts: redwood-cost-sim-v2.xlsx visible] Marcus Ng: first slide, assumptions: sequence lengths, kv entry size, cache TTL and hit distribution. note — transcription may show 'K V' sometimes, but it's KV cache — it's the same thing.
[02:20] Priya Shah: can you remind me quickly the difference between prefix and prefetch in your terminology? we use a different word in-house.
[02:26] Marcus Ng: sure — prefix caching is caching the output KV states that are common prefixes, so when the user continues the conversation the runtime reuses kv cache entries; prefetch is proactively warming the cache by issuing behind-the-scenes tokens for predicted next steps (or precomputing likely continuations) — so prefetch costs some background tokens but reduces on-demand latency and increases effective hit rate.
[02:49] Tomás Rivera: and how do you prevent prefetch from blowing our token budget if predictions are wrong?
[02:55] Marcus Ng: good point. we gate prefetch with heuristics: only prefetch on high-confidence triggers, and we cap prefetch concurrency per session. the sim lets you dial the prefetch aggressiveness and shows net token delta.

[03:11] [00:03:11 - Speaker label slips to Speaker 2 briefly] Speaker 2: uh mm-hmm
[03:15] Marcus Ng: ha, classic transcript artifact. anyway — scenario A: prefix-only with 60% effective hit rate. that reduces per-token compute by avoiding the early layers, so cost drops ~18% and p95 improves ~20% in our model.
[03:31] Ellen Park: 60% seems optimistic for us — clinical notes vary a lot. our reuse would be concentrated in templated sections though.
[03:38] Ivy Chen: totally, Priya, when you provide sample traces we can run with your actual prefix overlap distribution; the sim uses a default which we adjust.

[03:50] Marcus Ng: scenario B — prefetch conservative: prefetch hit rate bump to 75% but prefetch adds 6% background tokens. net cost reduction ~26%, p95 drop to ~70-80ms. scenario C aggressive prefetch and higher concurrency: 85% hit, 12% background tokens, net cost down ~34% but risk of wasted tokens if prediction is wrong.
[04:18] Priya Shah: ok so aggressive gets close to our 40% target but increases background tokens. what about batching — can we increase concurrency without hurting p95?
[04:26] Marcus Ng: yes, batching trades latency for throughput, but Redwood's continuous batching tries to balance using small windows and prioritizing low-latency requests. in the sim we model concurrency levels per GPU. going from 4 -> 8 concurrency improves token throughput costs ~10-12% but can increase p95 slightly. when combined with prefix/prefetch you often get compounding savings.

[04:48] Tomás Rivera: do you have numbers for 95th for the combined scenario? if we do prefetch conservative + concurrency 8?
[04:54] Marcus Ng: yes — conservative prefetch + concurrency 8 in the sim: net cost ~-30% vs baseline, p95 ~95 ms. note this assumes dedicated nodes (no noisy neighbor) and the optimized kernel selection we showed in the docs.

[05:11] Ellen Park: the 95ms is close to our 100ms target. what about tail risks if a big batch hits at once? our ingest window can spike 3x for 2 minutes.
[05:20] Lena Ortiz: we usually recommend burst capacity rules in Dedicated — autoscale + hot spare nodes. for Private deployments we can provision a small burst pool or route overflow to a compatible model with graceful degradation.
[05:33] Rashid Ahmed: routing is fine as long as audit logs show that the fallback data path doesn't leave our VPC.
[05:39] Ivy Chen: yep, in VPC deployment fallback stays in VPC; the control plane does not hold PII. we'll include the architecture diagram in the docs.

[05:53] Marcus Ng: back to the sim — another dimension is quantization. switching to 4-bit with quality testing yields another 8-14% cost improvement in many of our workloads, but for clinical extraction you'll want a quick quality eval. we can run Redwood Optimize evals against your prompt set.
[06:14] Priya Shah: quality regression is a non-starter if entity extraction drops recall. we'll need an A/B run on a holdout.
[06:19] Marcus Ng: agreed, sim can hook into your eval set; we'll output candidate configs and estimated quality delta.

[06:30] [06:30 - short cross-talk] Speakers: mm hmm, okay

[06:36] Marcus Ng: showing a live slider: hit rate vs prefetch cost. when you drag the prefetch aggressiveness from 0 to 1 you can see net per-token cost curve non-linear — early increases give big hit improvements. there's a sweet spot around 0.45 for templated clinical flows in our defaults.
[06:55] Tomás Rivera: can you annotate what that 0.45 corresponds to operationally? like how many background tokens per session?
[07:01] Marcus Ng: yep, that's about 2-4 background generations per session, capped at one per active user every 30s. so it's low enough to not explode budget but high enough to bootstrap sessions.

[07:14] Priya Shah: curious about metrics we should watch during pilot — besides p95 and token cost?
[07:19] Lena Ortiz: great question. we recommend: actual KV hit rate, prefetch waste rate (prefetches not used), per-session token overhead, end-to-end p99, and model quality metrics (precision/recall on extraction). also SLA breach count per day.

[07:37] Marcus Ng: i'll highlight one more sim output: concurrency sensitivity heatmap. it shows diminishing returns beyond concurrency 12 for this workload; also tail latency increases with naive batching. that's why we recommend adaptive batching windows and a TTL-based cache preference.

[07:55] Ellen Park: what's adaptive batching? we have strict SLOs and need deterministic behavior.
[08:00] Marcus Ng: adaptive batching is the runtime making micro-batching decisions based on current queue depth and latency budget; it will reduce batching when latency climbs above target. it's not black magic — values are tunable and we expose metrics.

[08:12] Tomás Rivera: we will need trace-level visibility and token-level billing breakdown; can your console show token cost per route and per model?
[08:19] Ivy Chen: yes, Redwood Console has per-route token and latency breakdowns, trace hooks, and you can correlate with request attributes. we'll show console screenshots in the follow-up pack.

[08:31] [08:31 - brief pause]

[08:35] Priya Shah: a few operational constraints: 1) data retention max 30 days for logs in our environment, 2) SSO via Okta, 3) must have RBAC for model access.
[08:44] Lena Ortiz: all standard — Okta SAML support, RBAC role templates, and configurable log retention. we'll include those configs.

[08:55] Marcus Ng: returning to the numbers: here's a sample pilot plan we propose — two-week pilot, ingest 3 days of traces to seed prefix distribution, then run A/B: 50% sessions on baseline fp16 concurrency 4, 50% on pilot config (prefetch conservative + concurrency 8 + optional 4-bit variant for non-critical steps). measure token delta and quality metrics.
[09:20] Tomás Rivera: how disruptive is pilot? requires DNS change or just routing?
[09:25] Ivy Chen: minimal. for Private we deploy Redwood runtime in your VPC and you route via internal endpoint, or for Dedicated we set up reserved nodes and provide endpoint. no DNS change if you use internal routing.

[09:37] Ellen Park: what about billing during pilot? we want clear line-item visibility, and if prefetch increases token counts we want caps.
[09:45] Lena Ortiz: during pilot we can set budget caps and alerting; we also share the simulated cost numbers upfront. pilot billing is usage-based but we'll provide daily dashboards.

[09:56] [Screen switches to example logs and sim output] Marcus Ng: here's a sample run with Avalon's anonymized traces (we replaced PII): baseline total tokens 1.2M/day, baseline cost estimate $Y/day, pilot config tokens 1.05M/day net (including prefetch), estimated 28% cost savings and p95 down to 92ms. aggressive config net tokens 980k/day but prefetch waste 9%.
[10:21] Priya Shah: those anonymized traces look close to ours. can you break out where savings come from?
[10:27] Marcus Ng: sure: ~50% of savings from KV reuse (prefix), ~25% from higher concurrency batching, ~25% from moving non-critical steps to quantized variants. prefetch itself contributes to an incremental hit rate improvement.

[10:41] Rashid Ahmed: curious about memory pressure on GPU when we keep more KV cached — is that a concern?
[10:46] Marcus Ng: yes you have a tradeoff — KV cache size per session can increase memory; we set soft TTLs and LRU eviction. the runtime can spill older KV to cheaper memory or restart partial contexts; for Dedicated we can right-size GPU memory or use instances with larger memory.

[10:59] Tomás Rivera: do you support eviction policies per route? we have different endpoints with varying reuse patterns.
[11:04] Ivy Chen: yes, per-route cache policy and per-route quantization mapping is supported via the config.

[11:12] Ellen Park: any compliance considerations with prefetch? since prefetch generates content, is that treated like user data?
[11:19] Lena Ortiz: good nuance — prefetch is treated as internal ephemeral computation; in Private deployments it remains in-customer environment. audit logs will show prefetch events. we can classify prefetch outputs as ephemeral and avoid persistence if required.

[11:35] Priya Shah: ok, so next steps to get the pilot on calendar: we need a pricing proposal and a technical runbook.
[11:41] Lena Ortiz: we'll send the pricing proposal tied to the simulated config plus pilot SOW. Marcus will send the runbook and sample k8s manifests for Private deployment.

[11:50] Marcus Ng: one more demo note — there's a feature we call 'session heatmap' in Console that shows where in sessions the cache hits concentrate; this helps tune prefetch aggressiveness per customer flow.
[12:03] Tomás Rivera: great, we'll want that.

[12:08] Priya Shah: do you have a rough estimate for engineering time to onboard the pilot? our infra team headcount is limited.
[12:14] Ivy Chen: onboarding is typically 2-5 engineer days for Private with a Redwood SA assisting. Dedicated is lighter because we manage the runtime. we can staff a Solutions Engineer for the first week.

[12:25] Ellen Park: what's the expected SLA during pilot?
[12:29] Lena Ortiz: we offer an initial pilot SLA of best-effort with monitoring; for production Dedicated we can back a 99.5% uptime SLA.

[12:36] [12:36 - short silence]

[12:38] Marcus Ng: i'll capture one operational recommendation: start conservative on prefetch, measure prefetch waste after 72 hours, then iterate. also adopt TTLs per endpoint and keep burst capacity for ingest windows.

[12:52] Priya Shah: that sounds reasonable.

[12:55] Marcus Ng: question from my side — do you have any locked-down models or regulatory constraints (e.g., model weights can't leave site)?
[13:02] Tomás Rivera: yes, for any PII we can't send weights outside; we prefer on-prem or in-VPC dedicated nodes. non-PII can use hosted variants for non-sensitive batch tasks.

[13:13] Ivy Chen: good, we'll draft an architecture that keeps PII compute on-prem and uses hosted for non-sensitive workloads only after approval.

[13:24] Ellen Park: any competitor-specific checks we should do? we are also evaluating Anthropic's hosted endpoint for latency.

[13:30] Lena Ortiz: competitors are fine — our differentiator is cost controls via batching/prefetch tooling and the unified runtime across Dedicated/Private. we'll include comparative notes.

[13:40] [13:40 - question bubble] Priya Shah: ok, final thought: can you include a quick runbook snippet for toggling prefetch aggressiveness in Console?
[13:47] Marcus Ng: yes — snippet will be in the follow-up pack, shows the UI slider and the API toggle.

[13:53] Lena Ortiz: great — to recap quickly: Marcus will send cost-sim spreadsheet and sample pilot config; Lena will send pricing and SOC2/DPA; Tomás will send QPS distribution and latencies; we target a pilot kickoff week of 2026-04-27 pending those items.

[14:12] Priya Shah: thanks all, that timeline works for us.
[14:16] Ellen Park: thanks Lena and team.

[14:19] Lena Ortiz: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with notes. bye.

[14:23] [call ends]

Note: timestamps in the transcript are approximate and labels occasionally mis-attributed due to automated transcription errors. Shared artifacts referenced: redwood-cost-sim-v2.xlsx (link to be emailed), pilot runbook and architecture diagram (to be shared).
